The engineers liked me 'cause I didn't get in their way and tell them how to do their job. I didn't stick around for mixing. I came in, played what I was told to play, collected my check, and left. Anyhow, they liked that and so they'd often recommend me. The pay was actually not bad. It just wasn't enough to live off, as it wasn't frequent enough. I'd then move to NC, and do much less studio work. I probably should have used that time to learn more about recording. Mostly, I showed up, went over the music, got a feel for what they wanted, and hit the booth until I was told I was done. No, this doesn't get your name on the credits. It's pretty common, actually. If you ever go that route, they'll want you to sign a few things away. One of those is an NDA. So, be prepared to be frustrated if you hear your work on the radio and can't discuss it.

Then, there's the performing parts of my life. Up until just ten years ago, I was pretty involved with music. I stayed a little involved since, but not like I was. I did this from about the age of 16 on, except for eight years - and I played through those, as well. I just wasn't in any paying gigs other than a few things like weddings. So, there's a snapshot of my life and a bit about what it was like. I don't get to make artistic calls when it's studio work, usually. Sometimes, they'd ask my input and I'd give it. But, I just did what I was told, mostly. Make sense?
